summary:
We built a search engine that finds places on Earth resembling a chosen location on Mars.

1) The user enters a Mars coordinate and their scientific objective in plain english. 
2) An LLM works out what they’re trying to do and picks the features that matter most. 3) The user can then review features by adding or removing, or change the weight of each feature. 
4) These features are then used to find analogs by measuring a weighted distance between Mars and Earth locations. We include delta checker to reject any match where a feature is too noisy to trust.

We combined open-source datasets onto one shared 5 km × 5 km grid and computed the same terrain features for both planets, so the two are directly comparable.

Our tool offers a new approach to early site scouting by cutting the time needed to search the whole planet.
details:
Martwin helps researchers find places on Earth that resemble a site on Mars for a specific scientific objective. The goal is to give NASA a shortlist of Earth locations to investigate for field studies and equipment tests, saving time before more detailed analysis or field visits. A researcher can start with any Mars coordinate and describe what they want to study in plain English. For example “Find a place where we could test a rover on terrain like the dunes at this site.”

We divided Earth and Mars into roughly 5 km × 5 km grid cells, covering about 20.4 million cells on Earth and 5.8 million on Mars. We gathered large datasets on elevation, dunes, valleys, soil, minerals, vegetation, temperature, and ice. Preparing the data took much of our time as the sources came in different formats which we had to align and calculate summary statistics for. We also calculated derived properties that no single source measured directly. For example, combining how much sunlight reaches a surface with how much it reflects lets us estimate how much energy the surface absorbs. We organized the results in our Starman dataset on Hugging Face.

We use INDUS, developed by NASA and IBM, as an embedding model to match the meaning of a user's objective to the measurements in our catalog. A language model then proposes how to compare those measurements by choosing certain representations like an average, or the standard deviation. This is because two cells can have the same average slope even if one is gently sloping throughout and the other alternates between flat ground and steep ridges. Standard deviation thus allows us to weigh in other factors like how much the slopes vary within each cell.

We rank candidates using a weighted Mahalanobis distance. Here, distance means how different two places are in the features we selected. We also added configurable weights for the user to change depending on what they aim to prioritize. We also factored in potential correlations between two features and tested an uncertainty check, delta, which asks whether a difference is large enough to trust given the limits of the data. Earth elevation maps can pick up treetops as a flat plain which delta helps counteract by determining that the region may not be eligible.

We used Python, NumPy, and Rasterio to process maps and calculate scores, Parquet to store the grid data, and Hugging Face cloud CPUs for large processing runs and scoring benchmarks. We built the interactive map with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet and connected it to a FastAPI backend.

The dataset we built also opens up for more broader search opportunities. In the future, researchers could ask the tool to find pairs of similar sites across Earth and Mars without choosing a Mars location first. We could also let teams give extra weight to practical factors on Earth, such as road access, nearby towns, and reliable supplies.
